views.markdown: Blocks network traffic as soon as the VPN connection drops. A background daemon watches the routing table: if the default route sits on a `utun` interface, the VPN counts as active. When it disappears, outbound traffic is cut off using blocking routes — for IPv4 and IPv6.
The daemon listens on the kernel routing socket and is notified by events rather than polling. The gap between drop and block is milliseconds.

- Blocks IPv4 and IPv6 independently
- Allow list for VPN servers so the VPN app can reconnect
- Detects server addresses on its own, adopting them after repeated confirmation
- Separate block list for permanently unreachable targets, including ranges like `17.0.0.0/8`
- Three blocking styles: interface-scoped, globally discarding, or rejecting
- App with a live per-interface traffic view, separated by direction
- Installation test and a shareable diagnostic report
- Pause for intentional disconnects, ends on its own once the tunnel is back
- Safety release: a block is lifted automatically after ten minutes without VPN

After installation the tweak runs in test mode and blocks nothing, so detection can be verified without risking a lockout.

1. Open the **Kill Switch** app
2. Connect the VPN, then tap **Learn**
3. Tap **Armed**
4. Disconnect the VPN and check the traffic monitor for outbound traffic

The app ships in English and German and follows the device language.
**Granularity.** Rules apply per destination address, not per app or port. That would require `pf` or a Network Extension, neither of which iOS offers here.
**Inbound.** Routes only control outbound traffic. Inbound packets still reach the interface but cannot be answered.
**System behaviour.** While blocking, iOS may report “no internet connection” and switch to cellular, where blocking also applies.
**VPN apps.** Some apps will not attempt a connection while the network is blocked. The pause function and an automatic reconnect window address this.

**Boot start repaired, on a corrected diagnosis.**

Earlier versions rewrote the LaunchDaemon plist with the resolved `/private/preboot/<hash>/dopamine-XXXXXX/...` path, believing launchd would not follow the `/var/jb` symlink and that this caused the EX_CONFIG (78) start failure. Measured on the device, that is wrong: launchd bootstraps the job over `/var/jb` without complaint, and every other jailbreak daemon — sshd, shshd, atrun — uses `/var/jb` too. The real cause was the missing directory behind `StandardOutPath`, which the repair tool also creates.

The resolved path was actively harmful: its random component is regenerated per jailbreak, so the plist pointed nowhere after a re-jailbreak.

- The plist stays as shipped; nothing rewrites it any more
- The boot script deleted no stale status file, so its launchctl-free fallback had been dead since it was written — `/var/run` survives a reboot, the file was always there, the check always said \u201calready running\u201d
- `launchctl` is a separate package on Dopamine and may be absent. Every call now checks first and says so instead of failing with 127 into a discarded stderr
- The daemon creates `var/run` and `var/log` itself. Missing, it ran but wrote neither status nor log — and every health check in this project reads that status file, so a healthy daemon looked dead
- A failed lock file no longer disables the instance lock silently
- The boot script sets an explicit PATH and detaches the daemon with `nohup`
- The installation test reported the old, wrong diagnosis and now reports the measured one
- Verified by a userspace reboot: launchd starts the daemon from the plist, the rc.d script does **not** run on Dopamine. The install message used to claim \u201cboot trigger installed\u201d, which was simply untrue. The script stays in the package because palera1n and older Procursus setups do run rc.d, and a double start is harmless.
- Stated plainly at install time: this covers a **userspace** reboot only. Dopamine is semi-untethered — after a full device reboot nothing under `/var/jb` runs until you re-run the Dopamine app.

- Detects network changes and reports them, so GG Status can show a banner: Wi-Fi \u2194 cellular \u2194 VPN, and joining a different Wi-Fi network
- The Wi-Fi name is read from the system configuration store. `SCDynamicStore` is marked unavailable in the iOS SDK but present in the framework, so the two functions needed are declared by hand — the same approach already used for the routing headers.
- `NET_NOTIFY=0` switches it off

- Learning VPN servers is far stricter. It used to take four confirmations in as many main-loop rounds — and the daemon is woken by routing events, so those four rounds passed in seconds, right while iOS pins push and iCloud connections to the physical interface. Three of four learned addresses on the test device belonged to Apple, Google and Azure, and each stayed reachable during a block. Now a candidate has to hold for four confirmations at least 30 s apart, spanning 2 minutes, after the tunnel has been up for a minute — and half-finished candidates are discarded when the tunnel cycles.
- The log is capped at 512 KB; when exceeded, the older half is dropped

- **Blocking works again.** Interface-scoped blocking used the loopback address as its gateway. Globally the kernel accepts that; bound to an interface it rejects the route with `ENETUNREACH`, because the gateway has to be reachable within that scope. Since `scoped` became the default, not a single block had been installed. The route now uses the interface's own gateway, and falls back to the link itself where there is no gateway address (cellular).
- Fixed a feedback loop: when only the daemon's own route messages arrived, the wait returned immediately and the main loop spun — thousands of iterations per second and a log grown to 1.6 MB.
- Repeated failures are logged at most once a minute
- `vpnkillswitch-fix` no longer aborts over a helper script removed in 3.9.0, which had stopped the daemon from being started at all

- App available in English and German; English is the default
- Daemon replies are localized in the app as well
- Terminal tools output English
- `vpnkillswitch-test` rewritten: it now checks routes instead of the `pf` setup the daemon no longer uses
- Removed four helper scripts that had become dead weight
- Diagnostic report is English throughout and now includes the GG Status log, if that tweak is installed

- Interface-scoped blocking is the default, so iOS keeps reporting a usable network and VPN apps still attempt to reconnect
- Reworked app layout, no more overlapping labels
Developed and tested on an iPhone 11 running iOS 18.6.2. Other devices and versions are unverified.
